newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIA'S BHP HOPES MANAGEMENT CRISIS BEHIND IT.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIA'S BHP HOPES MANAGEMENT CRISIS BEHIND IT.

text.p: Investors are expected on Monday to further punish Australian resources giant The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd (BHP) for a management crisis which sent the nation's bellwether stock tumbling last week.

BHP managing director John Prescott said on Sunday that last week's resignation of three executives had created some short-term difficulties for the resources giant, Australia's largest listed company.
Prescott said in a television interview that some tough decisions would have to be made to improve the performance of the company's existing assets as well as new projects.

On Friday, BHP announced that its petroleum division chief, John O'Connor, had resigned due to irreconcilable differences with the board. The resignation compounded market concern after the sudden departures of minerals division chief Dick Carter and iron ore head Geoff Wedlock during the previous two days.
More than A$2 billion (US$1.5 billion) was wiped off the value of BHP's shares last week after news of the resignations.
Prescott said he hoped the turmoil was behind the petroleum, steel and minerals giant, but added that the process of restoring investor confidence would be gradual.

"This is always difficult and yes, it will make things more difficult in the short term, but the company has a great depth of talent, great depth of strength and we'll get on with the task," Prescott said.

Analysts are tipping more downside for BHP's shares, which lost 45 cents to end at A$16.99 on Friday. They dragged the market benchmark All Ordinaries index 9.4 points lower to 2,717.7 after it appeard it would close steady. BHP shares fell 55 cents on Thursday.
BHP now has a capitalisation of A$34 billion.
"Things will get worse before they get better. BHP smells bad to institutions -- the odour will take a while to fade," a dealer at a Melbourne-based brokerage told Reuters.
One institutional market strategist said he believed the company's shares had been oversold but a recovery for the stock was unlikely to occur in the short-term.
"Clearly it has been very weak and a lot of the bad news has already been factored in but certain aspects are being sorted.
"But it's not going to turn around and go in the other direction quickly. There is still a lot of negative sentiment," the analyst said.
However, Prescott said he did not think the market had had the opportunity to objectively assess the situation.

"We are clearly focused on doing what has to be done to improve the performance of the company's existing assets, to see that we commission the new projects in line with expectations and that we apply a high standard of assessment to how further new proposals may work out," he said.
"In the process of doing all that we have to make some tough decisions," he said.

The resignation of O'Connor, a board director, was the biggest shock to the market. Widely touted as heir apparent to Prescott, O'Connor left due to "irreconcilable differences" with the the rest of the board.
Institutions and analysts regarded O'Connor highly and media speculated at the weekend that an investor backlash could lead to the ultimate ousting of Prescott and chairman Jerry Ellis.

Prescott and Ellis told a hastily convened news conference on Friday night that O'Connor's departure followed a long-term disagreement over the possible float of the profitable petroleum unit, a plan the board rejected several months ago.
Prescott said on Sunday BHP hoped the management crisis was behind it. "I hope there won't be any more turmoil," he said.
But he added: "... We are clearly in a situation where we have to address every aspect of the company's operations and we'll have some hard decisions to make, not all of them I hope, people related."
Minerals chief Carter's resignation on Wednesday coincided with a separate company statement about cost overruns at BHP's Pilbara hot briquetted iron (HBI) project in Western Australia.
Prescott linked Carter's exit with the management of the Pilbara HBI project and said the company strived to ensure its projects were under control.
The HBI plant was originally expected to cost A$1.2 billion but this estimate was revised up to A$1.65 billion. Analysts now speculate the final cost could be 10 percent higher still.
HBI is used as a feedstock in modern steel making.
BHP is expected to announce the results of a strategic review of its mineral assets within the next weeks.
Analysts said this review, which is expected to recommend a significant shake-up of the group's coal division, had the best potential to revive the group's share price.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
